title: I Inherited $300k in Stocks and Braced for a Huge Tax Bill. The Step-Up Erased Almost All of It.
summary: A step-up in basis can reduce most of the capital gains tax on inherited stocks, depending on when you sell.
body_markdown:
[Inheriting investments can trigger taxes](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/do-you-have-to-pay-taxes-on-inheritance-money) , but a step-up in basis may reduce what you owe when you sell. It generally applies to taxable assets like stocks and real estate, not retirement accounts or lifetime gifts. Here’s an example of a $300,000 stock inheritance, and how a step-up in basis could save you $37,500 in federal taxes.


## How a Step-Up in Basis Can Reduce Capital Gains on Inheritance


When you sell an investment,[capital gains tax](https://smartasset.com/investing/capital-gains-tax-calculator) is based on the difference between the sale price and[your cost basis](https://smartasset.com/investing/cost-basis) . For[inherited stocks](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/cost-basis-of-inherited-stock) , the basis is generally reset to[fair market value](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/fair-market-value) on the date of the original owner’s death.1 Growth that happened before the inheritance isn’t taxed when you sell.


Inherited stocks are also taxed at[long-term capital gains rates](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/short-term-vs-long-term-capital-gains) , even if you sell soon after inheriting them. In some cases, the executor can choose to value estate assets six months after death when alternate valuation rules are met. Separate rules also apply in[community property states](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/community-property-states) . A survivor can receive a step-up on both halves when the other owner dies.


The table shows how different types of inherited and gifted assets are taxed:


Type of Asset Tax Treatment


Inherited stocks Basis generally resets to fair market value at death


Gifted stocks Basis generally carries over from the giver, although special rules can apply when the property’s value has fallen


Inherited traditional IRA or 401(k) Withdrawals are generally taxed as ordinary income


Inherited Roth IRA Qualified withdrawals can be tax-free


In 2026, single filers pay a 0% long-term capital gains rate on taxable income up to $49,450, 15% up to $545,500 and 20% above that.2[Married couples filing jointly](https://smartasset.com/taxes/married-filing-jointly-vs-separately) pay 0% up to $98,900, 15% up to $613,700 and 20% above that. In 2027, those limits go up to $51,050 and $563,200 for single filers and to $102,100 and $633,600 for married couples filing jointly.3

## A Step-Up That Could Save $37,500 on Inherited Stocks


To calculate the potential tax impact on inherited stock, let’s assume that your parent bought stocks for $50,000 and they are worth $300,000 when they die. If you inherit them and sell soon after, your basis will generally be $300,000. This could eliminate most of the capital gain that built up during your parent’s lifetime.


The table compares four outcomes: selling right away, selling after the price goes up, selling after the price falls and selling inherited stock without a step-up in basis:


Scenario Original Purchase Price Value at Death Sale Price Tax Basis Taxable Gain or Loss Illustrative Federal Tax


Step-up; sold immediately $50,000 $300,000 $300,000 $300,000 $0 $0


Step-up; price rises before sale $50,000 $300,000 $330,000 $300,000 $30,000 gain $4,500


Step-up; price falls before sale $50,000 $300,000 $270,000 $300,000 $30,000 loss $0


No step-up $50,000 $300,000 $300,000 $50,000 $250,000 gain $37,500


The last row shows what the tax would look like if the original $50,000 basis carried over. Assuming the entire $250,000 gain falls in the 15% federal long-term capital gains bracket, you would pay $37,500 in taxes.


If the stocks climb to $330,000 after you inherit them, you would have a $30,000 gain. At a 15% long-term capital gains rate, your federal tax bill would be $4,500. A drop to $270,000 instead creates a $30,000 capital loss, with no capital gains tax owed on the sale.

## 3 Rules That Can Affect Your Inheritance Taxes


Selling[inherited stock](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/what-happens-to-stocks-when-you-die) can trigger more than capital gains tax. If your[modified adjusted gross (MAGI)](https://smartasset.com/taxes/what-is-modified-adjusted-gross-income) income tops $200,000 as a single filer, or $250,000 as a married couple filing jointly, you may also owe a 3.8%[net investment income tax (NIIT)](https://smartasset.com/investing/net-investment-income-tax) .4 Depending on where you live, your state may tax the gain as well.


Special basis rules can also affect how much of an inheritance is taxable. They apply to certain family farms, closely held businesses and land with conservation easements.


Another rule covers appreciated property that gets transferred shortly before death. If you or your spouse give it to someone who dies within a year, and that property then passes back to you, the original basis generally carries over and does not reset to market value.
